entries.d629149873a453e0226246c778d0cadd44fb2bb4: <div sID="gen24865" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Mark.13" sID="Mark.13"/> <div eID="gen24865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24866" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24867" type="x-p"/> We have here the substance of that prophetical sermon which our Lord Jesus preached, pointing at the destruction of Jerusalem, and the consummation of all things; it was one of the last of his sermons, and not <hi type="italic">ad populum</hi>—to the people, but <hi type="italic">ad clerum</hi>—to the clergy; it was private, preached only to four of his disciples, with whom his secret was. Here is, I. The occasion of his prediction—his disciples' admiring the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.1-Mark.13.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), and their enquiry concerning the time of the desolation of them, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.3-Mark.13.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. II. The predictions themselves, 1. Of the rise of deceivers, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.5-Mark.13.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.21-Mark.13.23">21-23</reference>. 2. Of the wars of the nations, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.7-Mark.13.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. 3. Of the persecution of Christians, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.9-Mark.13.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. 4. Of the destruction of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.14-Mark.13.20">ver. 14-20</reference>. 5. Of the end of the world, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.24-Mark.13.27">ver. 24-27</reference>. III. Some general intimations concerning the time of them, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.28-Mark.13.32">ver. 28-32</reference>. IV. Some practical inferences from all, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.33-Mark.13.37">ver. 33-37</reference>.
entries.b4c9495406e4e19b114c39d4846aca75b6c196fc: <div eID="gen24867" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24866" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of the Temple Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings <hi type="italic">are here!</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down. <hi type="super">3</hi> And as he sat upon the mount of Olives over against the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <hi type="super">4</hi> Tell us, when shall these things be? and what <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled? <div eID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> We may here see, <div eID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> I. How apt many of Christ's own disciples are to idolize things that look <hi type="italic">great,</hi> and have been long looked upon as <hi type="italic">sacred.</hi> They had heard Christ complain of those who had made the temple a <hi type="italic">den of thieves;</hi> and yet, when he quitted it, for the wickedness that remained in it, they court him to be as much in love as they were with the stately structure and adorning of it. One of them said to him, "Look, Master, <hi type="italic">what manner of stones, and what buildings are here,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">v. 1</reference>. We never saw the like in Galilee; O do not leave this fine place." <div eID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> II. How little Christ values external pomp, where there is not real purity; "<hi type="italic">Seest thou these great buildings</hi>" (saith Christ), "and admirest thou them? I tell thee, the time is at hand when <hi type="italic">there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.2">v. 2</reference>. And the sumptuousness of the fabric shall be no security to it, no nor move any compassion in the Lord Jesus towards it. He looks with <hi type="italic">pity</hi> upon the ruin of precious souls, and weeps over them, for on them he has put great value; but we do not find him look with any pity upon the ruin of a magnificent house, when he is driven out of it by sin, for that is of small value with him. With what little concern doth he say, <hi type="italic">Not one stone shall be left on another!</hi> Much of the strength of the temple lay in the largeness of the stones, and if these be thrown down, no footstep, no remembrance, of it will remain. While any part remained standing, there might be some hopes of the repair of it; but what hope is there, when not one stone is <hi type="italic">left upon another?</hi> <div eID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> III. How natural it is to us to desire to know things to come, and the times of them; more inquisitive we are apt to be about that than about our duty. His disciples knew not how to <hi type="italic">digest</hi> this doctrine of the ruin of the temple, which they thought must be their Master's royal palace, and in which they expected their preferment, and to have the posts of honour; and therefore they were in pain till they got him alone, and got more out of him concerning this matter. As he was returning to Bethany therefore, he <hi type="italic">sat upon the mount of Olives, over against the temple,</hi> where he had a full view of it; and there four of them agreed to <hi type="italic">ask him privately,</hi> what he meant by the destroying of the temple, which they understood no more than they did the predictions of his own death, so inconsistent was it with their scheme. Probably, though these four proposed the question, yet Christ's discourse, in answer to it, was in the hearing of the rest of the disciples, yet <hi type="italic">privately,</hi> that is, apart from the multitude. Their enquiry is, <hi type="italic">When shall these things be?</hi> They will not question, at least not seem to question, whether they shall be or no (for their Master has said that they shall), but are willing to hope it is a great way off. Yet they ask not precisely the day and year (therein they were modest), but say, "Tell us <hi type="italic">what shall be the sign, when all these things shall be fulfilled?</hi> What presages shall there be of them, and how may we prognosticate their approach?"
entries.013d20fab5e874fdb46f5b01d265541a8335071d: <div eID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Great Afflictions Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And Jesus answering them began to say, Take heed lest any <hi type="italic">man</hi> deceive you: <hi type="super">6</hi> For many shall come in my name, saying, I am <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> and shall deceive many. 7 And when ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, be ye not troubled: for <hi type="italic">such things</hi> must needs be; but the end <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> yet. <hi type="super">8</hi> For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be earthquakes in divers places, and there shall be famines and troubles: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the beginnings of sorrows. <hi type="super">9</hi> But take heed to yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them. 10 And the gospel must first be published among all nations. 11 But when they shall lead <hi type="italic">you,</hi> and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against <hi type="italic">their</hi> parents, and shall cause them to be put to death. <hi type="super">13</hi> And ye shall be hated of all <hi type="italic">men</hi> for my name's sake: but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. <div eID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus, in reply to their question, sets himself, not so much to satisfy their curiosity as to direct their consciences; leaves them still in the dark concerning the <hi type="italic">times</hi> and <hi type="italic">seasons,</hi> which the father has <hi type="italic">kept in his own power,</hi> and which <hi type="italic">it was not for them to know;</hi> but gives them the cautions which were needful, with reference to the events that should now shortly come to pass. <div eID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> I. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> by the <hi type="italic">seducers</hi> and <hi type="italic">imposters</hi> that should now shortly arise (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.5-Mark.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Take heed lest any man deceive you,</hi> lest, having found the <hi type="italic">true Messiah,</hi> you lose him again in the crowd of <hi type="italic">pretenders,</hi> or be inveigled to embrace others in rivalship with him. Many shall come <hi type="italic">in my name</hi> (not in the name of <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi>), but saying, <hi type="italic">I am the Christ,</hi> and so claiming the dignities which I only an entitled to." After the Jews had rejected the true Christ, they were imposed upon, and so <hi type="italic">ex</hi>posed by many false Christs, but never before; those false Christs <hi type="italic">deceived many;</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">take heed lest they deceive you.</hi> Note, When many are deceived, we should thereby be awakened to look to ourselves. <div eID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> II. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">disturbed</hi> at the noise of wars, which they should be alarmed with, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.7-Mark.13.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Sin introduced <hi type="italic">wars,</hi> and they come <hi type="italic">from men's lusts.</hi> But at some times the nations are more distracted and wasted with wars than at other times; so it shall be now; Christ was born into the world when there was a general peace, but soon after he went out of the world there were general wars; <hi type="italic">Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.</hi> And what will become of them then who are to preach the gospel to every nation? <hi type="italic">Inter arma silent leges—Amidst the clash of arms, the voice of law is not heard.</hi> "But <hi type="italic">be not troubled at it.</hi>" 1. "Let it be no <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> to you; you are bid to expect it, and <hi type="italic">such things must needs be,</hi> for God has appointed them, in order to further accomplishment of his purposes, and by the <hi type="italic">wars of the Jews</hi>" (which Josephus has given us a large account of) "God will punish the <hi type="italic">wickedness of the Jews.</hi>" 2. "Let it be no <hi type="italic">terror</hi> to you, as if your interest were in danger of being overthrown, or your work obstructed by these wars; you have no concern in them, and therefore need not be apprehensive of any damage by them." Note, Those that despise the smiles of the world, and do not court and covet them, may despise the frowns of the world, and need not fear them. If we seek not to rise with them that <hi type="italic">rise in the world,</hi> why should we dread falling with them that fall in the world? 3. "Let it not be looked upon as an omen of the approaching period of the world, for the <hi type="italic">end is not yet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.7">v. 7</reference>. Think not that these <hi type="italic">wars</hi> will bring the world to a period; no, there are other intermediate counsels to be fulfilled betwixt that end and the end of all things, which are designed to prepare you for the end, but not to hasten it out of due time." 4. "Let it not be looked upon as if in them God has done his worst; no, he has more arrows in his quiver, and they are <hi type="italic">ordained against the persecutors;</hi> be not troubled at the wars you shall hear of, for they are but <hi type="italic">the beginnings of sorrows,</hi> and therefore, instead of being disturbed at <hi type="italic">them,</hi> you ought to <hi type="italic">prepare for worse;</hi> for there shall also be <hi type="italic">earthquakes in divers places,</hi> which shall bury multitudes in the ruins of their own houses, and there <hi type="italic">shall be famines,</hi> by which many of the poor shall perish for want of bread, and <hi type="italic">troubles</hi> and commotions; so that there shall be no peace to him that <hi type="italic">goes out</hi> or <hi type="italic">comes in.</hi> The world shall be full of <hi type="italic">troubles,</hi> but <hi type="italic">be not ye troubled;</hi> without are <hi type="italic">fightings,</hi> within are <hi type="italic">fears,</hi> but <hi type="italic">fear not ye their fear.</hi>" Note, The disciples of Christ, if it be not their own fault, may enjoy a holy security and serenity of mind, when all about them is in the greatest disorder. <div eID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> III. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">drawn away</hi> from Christ, and from their duty to him, by the sufferings they should meet with for Christ's sake. Again, he saith, "<hi type="italic">Take heed to yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.9">v. 9</reference>. Though you may escape the <hi type="italic">sword of war,</hi> better than some of your neighbours, because you interest not yourselves in the public quarrels, yet be not secure; you will be exposed to the <hi type="italic">sword of justice</hi> more than others, and the parties that contend with one another, will unite against you. <hi type="italic">Take heed</hi> therefore lest you <hi type="italic">deceive</hi> yourselves with the hopes of outward prosperity, and such a temporal kingdom as you have been dreaming of, when it is <hi type="italic">through many tribulations</hi> that <hi type="italic">you must enter into the kingdom of God.</hi> Take heed lest you needlessly expose yourselves to trouble, and pull it upon your own head. <hi type="italic">Take heed</hi> what you say and do, for you will have many eyes upon you." Observe, <div eID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> 1. What the trouble is which they must expect. <div eID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> (1.) They shall be <hi type="italic">hated of all men;</hi> trouble enough! The thoughts of <hi type="italic">being hated</hi> are grievous to a tender spirit, and the fruits of that hatred must needs be a constant vexation; those that are <hi type="italic">malicious,</hi> will be <hi type="italic">mischievous.</hi> It was not for any thing amiss in them, or done amiss by them, that they were <hi type="italic">hated,</hi> but for Christ's name sake, because they were called by his name, called upon his name, preached his name, and wrought miracles in his name. The world hated them because he loved them. <div eID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their own <hi type="italic">relations</hi> shall <hi type="italic">betray them,</hi> those to whom they were most nearly allied, and on whom therefore they depended for protection; "They <hi type="italic">shall betray you,</hi> shall inform against you, and be your prosecutors." If a father has a child that is a Christian, he shall become void of natural affection, it shall be swallowed up in bigotry, and he shall betray his own child to the persecutors, as if he were a worshipper of other gods, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6-Deut.13.10">Deut. xiii. 6-10</reference>. <div eID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their <hi type="italic">church-rulers</hi> shall inflict <hi type="italic">their censures</hi> upon them; "You shall be <hi type="italic">delivered up</hi> to the great Sanhedrim at Jerusalem, and to the inferior courts and consistories in other cities, and shall be <hi type="italic">beaten in the synagogues</hi> with forty stripes at a time, as offenders against the law which was read in the synagogue." It is no new thing for the church's artillery, through the treachery of its officers, to be turned against some of its best friends. <div eID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> (4.) <hi type="italic">Governors</hi> and <hi type="italic">kings</hi> shall use their power against them. Because the Jews have not power to put them to death, they shall incense the Roman powers against them, as they did Herod against James and Peter; and they shall <hi type="italic">cause you to be put to death,</hi> as enemies to the empire. They must resist unto blood, and still resist. <div eID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> 2. What they shall have to comfort themselves with, in the midst of these great and sore troubles. <div eID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> (1.) That the work they were called to should be carried on and prosper, notwithstanding all this opposition which they should meet with in it (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.10">v. 10</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The gospel</hi> shall, for all this, be <hi type="italic">published among all nations,</hi> and before the destruction of Jerusalem the <hi type="italic">sound</hi> of it shall <hi type="italic">go forth into all the earth;</hi> not only through all the nation of the Jews, but to all the nations of the earth." It is comfort to those who suffer for the gospel, that, though they may be crushed and borne down, the gospel cannot; it shall keep its ground, and carry the day. <div eID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> (2.) That their sufferings, instead of obstructing their work, should forward it; "Your being <hi type="italic">brought before governors and kings</hi> shall be for <hi type="italic">a testimony of them</hi> (so some read it, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.9">v. 9</reference>); it shall give you an opportunity of preaching the gospel to those before whom you are brought as criminals, to whom otherwise you could not have access." Thus St. Paul's being brought before Felix, and Festus, and Agrippa, and Nero, was a testimony to them concerning Christ and his gospel. Or, as we read it, It shall be for a testimony <hi type="italic">against them,</hi> against both the judges and the prosecutors, who pursue those with the utmost rage that appear, upon examination, to be not only innocent but excellent persons. The gospel is a testimony to us concerning Christ and heaven. If we receive it, it will be a testimony for us: it will justify and save us; if not, it will be a testimony <hi type="italic">against</hi> us in the great day. <div eID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> (3.) That, when they were brought before kings and governors for Christ's sake, they should have special assistance from heaven, to plead Christ's cause and their own (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.11">v. 11</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Take no thought before-hand what he shall speak,</hi> be not solicitous how to address yourselves to great men, so as to obtain their favour; your cause is just and glorious, and needs not be supported by premeditated speeches and harangues; but <hi type="italic">whatsoever shall be given you in that hour,</hi> whatsoever shall be suggested to you, and put into your minds, and into your mouths" (<hi type="italic">pro re nat&#226;—on the spur of the occasion</hi>), "that <hi type="italic">speak ye,</hi> and fear not the success of it, because it is <hi type="italic">off-hand,</hi> for <hi type="italic">it is not ye that speak,</hi> purely by the strength of your own wisdom, consideration, and resolution, but it is <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost.</hi>" Note, Those whom Christ calls out to be advocates for him, shall be furnished with full instructions: and when we are engaged in the service of Christ, we may depend upon the aids of the Spirit of Christ. <div eID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> (4.) That heaven at last would <hi type="italic">make amends for all;</hi> "You will meet with a great deal of hardship in your way, but have a good heart on it, your warfare will be accomplished, and your testimony finished, and <hi type="italic">he that shall endure to the end, the same shall be saved,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.13">v. 13</reference>. Perseverance gains the crown. The salvation here promised is more than a deliverance from evil, it is an everlasting blessedness, which shall be an abundant recompence for all their services and sufferings. All this we have, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.17">Matt. x. 17</reference>, &c.
entries.d3b79e9bcb9ce9b151c1695c368022a141f4a382: <div eID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of the Temple Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> But when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not, (let him that readeth understand,) then let them that be in Judæa flee to the mountains: <hi type="super">15</hi> And let him that is on the housetop not go down into the house, neither enter <hi type="italic">therein,</hi> to take any thing out of his house: <hi type="super">16</hi> And let him that is in the field not turn back again for to take up his garment. <hi type="super">17</hi> But woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days! <hi type="super">18</hi> And pray ye that your flight be not in the winter. <hi type="super">19</hi> For <hi type="italic">in</hi> those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created unto this time, neither shall be. <hi type="super">20</hi> And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days. <hi type="super">21</hi> And then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here <hi type="italic">is</hi> Christ; or, lo, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> there; believe <hi type="italic">him</hi> not: <hi type="super">22</hi> For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall show signs and wonders, to seduce, if <hi type="italic">it were</hi> possible, even the elect. <hi type="super">23</hi> But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things. <div eID="gen24888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24889" type="x-p"/> The Jews, in rebelling against the Romans, and in persecuting the Christians, were hastening to their own ruin apace, both efficiently and meritoriously, were setting both God and man against them; see <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15</reference>. Now here we have a prediction of that ruin which came upon them within less than forty years after this: we had it before, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Matt. xxiv. 15</reference>, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen24889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24890" type="x-p"/> I. What is here foretold concerning it. <div eID="gen24890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24891" type="x-p"/> 1. That the Roman <hi type="italic">armies</hi> should make a descent upon Judea, and invest Jerusalem, the holy city. These were the <hi type="italic">abomination</hi> of <hi type="italic">desolation,</hi> which the Jews did <hi type="italic">abominate,</hi> and by which they should be made <hi type="italic">desolate.</hi> The country of thine enemy is called <hi type="italic">the land which thou abhorrest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Isa. vii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> it was an abomination, because it brought with it nothing but desolation. They had rejected Christ as an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> who would have been their <hi type="italic">salvation;</hi> and now God brought upon them an abomination that would be their <hi type="italic">desolation,</hi> thus spoken of by Daniel <hi type="italic">the prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.27">ch. ix. 27</reference>), as that by which this sacrifice and offering should be made to cease. This army stood <hi type="italic">where it ought not,</hi> in and about the <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> which the heathen ought not to have approached, nor would have been suffered to approach, if Jerusalem had not first profaned the crown of their holiness. This the church complains of, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.10">Lam. i. 10</reference>, The <hi type="italic">heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command that they should not enter into the congregation;</hi> but sin made the breach, at which the glory went out, and the abomination of desolation broke in, <hi type="italic">and stood where it ought not.</hi> Now, let <hi type="italic">him that readeth</hi> this, <hi type="italic">understand it,</hi> and endeavor to take it right. Prophecies should not be too plain, and yet intelligible to those that search them; and they are best understood by comparing them first with one another, and at last with the event. <div eID="gen24891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24892" type="x-p"/> 2. That when the Roman <hi type="italic">army</hi> should come into the country, there would be no safety any where but by quitting the country, and that with all possible expedition. It will be in vain to <hi type="italic">fight,</hi> the enemies will be too hard for them; in vain to <hi type="italic">abscond,</hi> the enemies will find them out; and in vain to <hi type="italic">capitulate,</hi> the enemies will give them no quarter; a man cannot have so much as his life given him for a prey, but by <hi type="italic">fleeing to the mountains</hi> out of Judea; and let him take the first alarm, and make the best of his way. If he be <hi type="italic">on the house-top,</hi> trying from thence to discover the motions of the enemy, and spies them coming, let him not <hi type="italic">go down, to take any thing out of the house,</hi> for it will occasion his losing of time, which is more precious than his best goods, and will but encumber him, and embarrass his flight. If he be in the field, and there discover the approach of the enemy, let him get away as he is, and not <hi type="italic">turn back again, to take up his garment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.16">v. 16</reference>. If he can save his life, let him reckon it is a good bargain, though he can save nothing else, and be thankful to God, that, though he is cut short, he is not cut off. <div eID="gen24892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24893" type="x-p"/> 3. That it would go very hard at that time with poor mothers and nurses (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.17">v. 17</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Woe to them that are with child,</hi> that dare not go into strange places, that cannot shift for themselves, nor make haste as others can. And <hi type="italic">woe to them that give suck,</hi> that know not how either to leave the tender infants behind them, or to carry them along with them." Such is the vanity of the creature, that the time may often be, when the greatest comforts may prove the greatest burthens. It would likewise be very uncomfortable, if they should be forced to flee <hi type="italic">in the winter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.18">v. 18</reference>), when the <hi type="italic">weather</hi> and <hi type="italic">ways</hi> were bad, when the roads would be scarcely passable, especially in the mountains to which they must flee. If there be no remedy but that trouble must come, yet we may desire and pray that, if it be God's will, the circumstances of it may be so ordered as to be a mitigation of the trouble; and when things are bad, we ought to consider they might have been worse. It is bad to be forced to flee, but it would have been worse if it had been <hi type="italic">in the winter.</hi> <div eID="gen24893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24894" type="x-p"/> 4. That throughout all the country of the Jews, there should be such destruction and desolation made, as could not be paralleled in any history (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">In those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning</hi> of time; that is, <hi type="italic">of the creation which God created,</hi> for time and the creation are of equal date, <hi type="italic">unto this day, neither shall be</hi> to the end of time; such a complication of miseries, and of such continuance. The destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans was very terrible, but this exceeded it. It threatened a universal slaughter of all the people of the Jews; so barbarously did they devour one another, and the Romans devour them all, that, if their wars had continued a little longer, <hi type="italic">no flesh could have been saved,</hi> not one Jew could have been left alive; but in the midst of wrath God remembered mercy; and, (1.) He <hi type="italic">shortened the days;</hi> he let fall his controversy before he had <hi type="italic">made a full end.</hi> As a church and nation the ruin was complete, but many particular persons had their lives given them for a prey, by the storm's subsiding when it did. 2. It was <hi type="italic">for the elects' sake</hi> that those days were shortened; <hi type="italic">many</hi> among them fared the better for the sake of the <hi type="italic">few</hi> among them that believed in Christ, and were faithful to him. There was a promise, that <hi type="italic">a remnant</hi> should be saved (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa. x. 22</reference>), and that God would not, for his servants' sakes, <hi type="italic">destroy them all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.8">Isa. lxvi. 8</reference>); and these promises must be fulfilled. God's own <hi type="italic">elect cry day and night to him,</hi> and their prayers must be answered, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">Luke xviii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen24894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24895" type="x-p"/> II. What directions are given to the disciples with reference to it. <div eID="gen24895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24896" type="x-p"/> 1. They must shift for the safety of <hi type="italic">their lives;</hi> "When you see the country invaded, and the city invested, flatter not yourselves with thoughts that the enemy will retire, or that you may be able to make your part good with them; but, without further deliberation or delay, <hi type="italic">let them that are in Judea, flee to the mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.14">v. 14</reference>. Meddle not with the strife that <hi type="italic">belongs not to you; let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth,</hi> but do you go out of the ship when you see it sinking, that you die not the <hi type="italic">death of the uncircumcised</hi> in heart." <div eID="gen24896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24897" type="x-p"/> 2. They must provide for the safety of <hi type="italic">their souls;</hi> "<hi type="italic">Seducers</hi> will be busy at that time, for they love to fish in troubled waters, and therefore then you must double your guard; <hi type="italic">then, if any man shall</hi> say unto you, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there,</hi> you know he is in heaven, and will come again at the end of time, to judge the world, and therefore <hi type="italic">believe them not;</hi> having received <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> be not drawn into the snares of any <hi type="italic">antichrist;</hi> for <hi type="italic">false Christs,</hi> and <hi type="italic">false prophets, shall arise,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.22">v. 22</reference>. When the gospel kingdom was in the setting up, Satan mustered all his force, to oppose it, and made use of all his wiles; and God permitted it, for the trial of sincerity of some, and the discovery of the hypocrisy of others, and the confusion of those who rejected Christ, when he was offered to them. <hi type="italic">False Christs</hi> shall <hi type="italic">rise,</hi> and false prophets that shall preach them up; or such, as, though they pretend not to be Christs, set up for <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> and undertake to foretel things to come, and they shall <hi type="italic">show signs</hi> and lying <hi type="italic">wonders;</hi> so early did the <hi type="italic">mystery of iniquity</hi> begin to <hi type="italic">work,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2 Thess. ii. 7</reference>. They <hi type="italic">shall seduce, if it were possible, the very elect;</hi> so plausible shall their pretences be, and so industrious shall they be to impose upon people, that they shall drawn away many that were forward and zealous professors of religion, many that were very likely to have persevered; for nothing will be effectual to secure men but that foundation of God which stands immovably sure, <hi type="italic">The Lord knoweth them that are his,</hi> who shall be preserved when the faith of some is overthrown, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18-2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 18, 19</reference>. They <hi type="italic">shall seduce, if it were possible, the very elect;</hi> but it is not possible to seduce them; the <hi type="italic">election shall obtain,</hi> whoever are <hi type="italic">blinded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>. But, in consideration hereof, let the disciples be cautious whom they give credit to (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.23">v. 23</reference>); But <hi type="italic">take ye heed.</hi> Christ knew that they were of the <hi type="italic">elect,</hi> who could not possibly be <hi type="italic">seduced,</hi> and yet he said to them, <hi type="italic">Take heed.</hi> An assurance of persevering, and cautions against apostasy, will very well consist with each other. Though Christ said to them, <hi type="italic">Take heed,</hi> it doth not therefore follow, that their perseverance was doubtful, for they were kept by the power of God; and though their perseverance was secured, yet it doth not therefore follow, that this caution was needless, because they must be kept in the use of proper means. God will keep them, but they must keep themselves. "<hi type="italic">I have foretold you all things;</hi> have foretold you of this danger, that, being <hi type="italic">fore-warned,</hi> you may be <hi type="italic">fore-armed;</hi> I have foretold <hi type="italic">all things</hi> which you needed to have foretold to you, and therefore take heed of hearkening to such as pretend to be prophets, and to foretel more than I have foretold." The sufficiency of the scripture is good argument against listening to such as pretend to inspiration.
entries.f30dfdd44837f4d7ced50dbdad889ed7940df38d: <div eID="gen24897" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Afflictions of the Jews Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24898" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, 25 And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken. <hi type="super">26</hi> And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. 27 And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven. <div eID="gen24898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24899" type="x-p"/> These verses seem to point at Christ's second coming, to judge the world; the disciples, in their question, had confounded the <hi type="italic">destruction</hi> of Jerusalem and the <hi type="italic">end of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.3">Matt. xxiv. 3</reference>), which was built upon a mistake, as if the temple must needs stand as long as the world stands; this mistake Christ rectifies, and shows that the <hi type="italic">end of the world in those days,</hi> those other days you enquire about, the day of Christ's coming, and the day of judgment, shall be <hi type="italic">after that tribulation,</hi> and not coincident with it. Let those who live to see the Jewish nation destroyed, take heed of thinking that, because the Son of man doth not visibly come in the clouds <hi type="italic">then,</hi> he will never <hi type="italic">so</hi> come; no, he will come <hi type="italic">after that.</hi> And here he foretels, <div eID="gen24899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24900" type="x-p"/> 1. The final dissolution of the present frame and fabric of the world; even of that part of it which seems least liable to change, the upper part, the pure and more refined part; <hi type="italic">The sun shall be darkened,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">moon</hi> shall no more <hi type="italic">give her light;</hi> for they shall be quite outshone by the glory of the Son of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa. xxiv. 23</reference>. The <hi type="italic">stars of heaven,</hi> that from the beginning had kept their place and regular motion, shall fall as leaves in autumn; and the <hi type="italic">powers that are in heaven,</hi> the heavenly bodies, the fixed stars, <hi type="italic">shall be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen24900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> 2. The visible appearance of the Lord Jesus, to whom the judgment of that day shall be committed (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.26">v. 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds.</hi> Probably he will come over that very place where he sat when he said this; for the clouds are in the lower region of the air. He shall come with <hi type="italic">great power and glory,</hi> such as will be suited to the errand on which he comes. <hi type="italic">Every eye shall then see him.</hi> <div eID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24902" type="x-p"/> 3. The gathering together of all the elect to him (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.27">v. 27</reference>); He shall <hi type="italic">send his angels,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gather together his elect</hi> to him, to <hi type="italic">meet him in the air,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">1 Thess. iv. 17</reference>. They shall be fetched from one end of the world to the other, so that none shall be missing from that <hi type="italic">general</hi> assembly; they shall be fetched <hi type="italic">from the uttermost part of the earth,</hi> most remote from the places where Christ's tribunal shall be set, and shall be brought to the <hi type="italic">uttermost part of heaven;</hi> so sure, so swift, so easy, shall their conveyance be, that there shall none of them miscarry, though they were to be brought from the uttermost part of the earth one way, to the uttermost part of the heaven another way. A faithful Israelite shall be carried safely, though it were from the utmost border of the land of bondage to the utmost border of the land of promise.
entries.713b479c5166f10bae132bc1b89efd05e6652e22: <div eID="gen24902" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Watchfulness Inculcated.</title> <div sID="gen24903" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near: <hi type="super">29</hi> So ye in like manner, when ye shall see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, <hi type="italic">even</hi> at the doors. <hi type="super">30</hi> Verily I say unto you, that this generation shall not pass, till all these things be done. <hi type="super">31</hi> Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away. <hi type="super">32</hi> But of that day and <hi type="italic">that</hi> hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father. <hi type="super">33</hi> Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is. 34 <hi type="italic">For the Son of man is</hi> as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch. 35 Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning: <hi type="super">36</hi> Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. <hi type="super">37</hi> And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch. <div eID="gen24903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> We have here the application of this prophetical sermon; <hi type="italic">now learn</hi> to look forward in a right manner. <div eID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24905" type="x-p"/> I. "As to the <hi type="italic">destruction</hi> of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">expect</hi> it to come very <hi type="italic">shortly;</hi> as when the <hi type="italic">branch of the fig-tree becomes soft,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">leaves sprout forth,</hi> ye expect that summer will come shortly, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.28">v. 28</reference>. When second causes begin to work, ye expect their effects in their proper order and time. So when <hi type="italic">ye see these things come to pass,</hi> when ye see the Jewish nation embroiled in wars, distracted by false Christs and prophets, and drawing upon them the displeasure of the Romans, especially when ye see them persecuting you for your Master's sake, and thereby standing to what they did when they put him to death, and repeating it, and so filling up the measure of their iniquity, then say that their <hi type="italic">ruin is nigh, even at the door,</hi> and provide for yourselves accordingly." The disciples themselves were indeed all of them, except John, taken away from the evil to come, but the next generation whom they were to train up, would live to see it; and by these instructions which Christ left behind him would be kept from sharing in it; "<hi type="italic">This generation</hi> that is now rising up, shall not all be worn off before <hi type="italic">all these things</hi> come to pass, which I have told you of, relating to Jerusalem, and they shall begin to take effect now shortly. And as this destruction is near and within ken, so it is sure. The decree is gone forth, it is a <hi type="italic">consummation determined,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>. Christ doth not speak these things, merely to frighten them; no, they are declarations of God's fixed purpose; "<hi type="italic">Heaven and earth shall pass away,</hi> at the end of time; but <hi type="italic">my words shall not pass away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.31">v. 31</reference>), not one of these predictions shall fail of a punctual accomplishment." <div eID="gen24905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24906" type="x-p"/> II. "As to the <hi type="italic">end of the world,</hi> do not enquire when it will come, for it is not a question fit to be asked, for of <hi type="italic">that day,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that hour, knoweth no man;</hi> it is a thing at a great distance; the exact time is fixed in the counsel of God, but is not revealed by any word of God, either to <hi type="italic">men</hi> on earth, or to <hi type="italic">angels in heaven;</hi> the angels shall have timely notice to prepare to attend in that day, and it shall be published, when it comes to the children of men, with sound of trumpet; but, at present, <hi type="italic">men</hi> and <hi type="italic">angels</hi> are kept in the dark concerning the precise time of it, that they may both attend to their proper services in the present day." But it follows, <hi type="italic">neither the Son;</hi> but is there any thing which the Son is ignorant of? We read indeed of a book which was sealed, till the Lamb opened the seals; but did not he know what was in it, before the seals were opened? Was not he privy to the writing of it? There were those in the primitive times, who taught from this text, that there were some things that Christ, as man, was <hi type="italic">ignorant</hi> of; and from these were called <hi type="italic">Agnoetæ;</hi> they said, "It was no more absurd to say so, than to say that his human soul suffered grief and fear;" and many of the orthodox fathers approved of this. Some would evade it, by saying that Christ spoke this in a way of prudential economy, to divert the disciples from further enquiry: but to this one of the ancients answers, <hi type="italic">It is not fit to speak too nicely in this matter</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou dei pany akribologein</hi></hi>, so Leontius in Dr. Hammond, "It is certain (says Archbishop Tillotson) that Christ, as God, could not be ignorant of any thing; but the divine wisdom which dwelt in our Saviour, did communicate itself to his human soul, according to the divine pleasure, so that his human nature might sometimes not know some things; therefore Christ is said to grow in wisdom (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Luke ii. 52</reference>), which he could not be said to do, if the human nature of Christ did necessarily know all things by virtue of its union with the divinity." Dr. Lightfoot explains it thus; Christ calls himself the Son, as Messiah. Now the Messiah, as such, was the father's servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>), sent and deputed by him, and as such a one he refers himself often to his Father's will and command, and owns he <hi type="italic">did nothing of himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">John v. 19</reference>); in like manner he might be said to <hi type="italic">know nothing of himself.</hi> The revelation of Jesus Christ was what <hi type="italic">God gave unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>. He thinks, therefore, that we are to distinguish between those excellencies and perfections of his, which resulted from the personal union between the divine and human nature, and those which flowed from the anointing of the Spirit; from the former flowed the infinite dignity of his perfect freedom from all sin; but from the latter flowed his power of working miracles, and his foreknowledge of things to come. What therefore (saith he) was to be revealed by him to his church, he was pleased to take, not from the union of the human nature with the divine, but from the revelation of the Spirit, by which he yet knew not this, but <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> only knows it; that is, God only, the Deity; for (as Archbishop Tillotson explains it) it is not used here <hi type="italic">personally,</hi> in distinction from the Son and the Holy Ghost, but as the Father is, <hi type="italic">Fons et Principium Deitatis</hi>—<hi type="italic">The Fountain of Deity.</hi> <div eID="gen24906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24907" type="x-p"/> III. "As to both, your duty is to <hi type="italic">watch and pray.</hi> Therefore the time is kept a secret, that you may be engaged to stand always upon your guard (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.33">v. 33</reference>); <hi type="italic">Take ye heed</hi> of every thing that would indispose you for your Master's coming, and would render your accounts <hi type="italic">perplexed,</hi> and your spirits so too; <hi type="italic">watch</hi> for his coming, that it may not at any time be a surprise to you, and <hi type="italic">pray</hi> for that grace which is necessary to qualify you for it, for <hi type="italic">ye know not when the time is;</hi> and you are concerned to be ready for that <hi type="italic">every day,</hi> which may come <hi type="italic">any day.</hi>" This he illustrates, in the close, by a parable. <div eID="gen24907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24908" type="x-p"/> 1. Our Master is gone away, and left us something in trust, in charge, which we must give account of, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.34">v. 34</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">as a man taking a far journey;</hi> for he is gone to be away a great while, he has <hi type="italic">left his house</hi> on earth, and left his servants in their offices, given <hi type="italic">authority</hi> to some, who are to be overseers, and <hi type="italic">work</hi> to others, who are to be labourers. They that have <hi type="italic">authority</hi> given them, in that had <hi type="italic">work</hi> assigned them, for those that have the greatest <hi type="italic">power</hi> have the most <hi type="italic">business;</hi> and to them to whom he gave <hi type="italic">work,</hi> he gave some sort of <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> to do that work. And when he took his last leave, he <hi type="italic">appointed the porter to watch,</hi> to be sure to be ready to open to him at his return; and in the mean time to take care to whom he opened his gates, not to thieves and robbers, but only to his Master's friends and servants. Thus our Lord Jesus, when he <hi type="italic">ascended on high,</hi> left something for all his servants to do, expecting they should all do him service in his absence, and be ready to receive him at his return. <hi type="italic">All</hi> are appointed to work, and some authorized to rule. <div eID="gen24908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24909" type="x-p"/> 2. We ought to be always upon our watch, in expectation of his return, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.35-Mark.13.37">v. 35-37</reference>. (1.) Our Lord <hi type="italic">will come,</hi> and will come as the <hi type="italic">Master of the house,</hi> to take account of his servants, of their work, and of the improvement they have made. (2.) We know not <hi type="italic">when he will come;</hi> and he has very wisely kept us at uncertainty, that we might all be always ready. We know not <hi type="italic">when he will come,</hi> just at what precise time; the <hi type="italic">Master of the house</hi> perhaps will come <hi type="italic">at even,</hi> at nine at night; or it may be <hi type="italic">at midnight,</hi> or a <hi type="italic">cock-crowing,</hi> at three in the morning, or perhaps not until six. This is applicable to his coming to us in particular, at our death, as well as to the general judgment. Our present life is a <hi type="italic">night,</hi> a dark night, compared with the other life; we know not in which watch of the night our Master will come, whether in the days of youth, or middle age, or old age; but, as soon as we are born, we begin to die, and therefore, as soon as we are capable of expecting any thing, we must expect death. (3.) Our great care must be, that, whenever our Lord comes, he do not <hi type="italic">find us sleeping,</hi> secure in ourselves, off our guard, indulging ourselves in ease and sloth, mindless of our work and duty, and thoughtless of our Lord's coming; <hi type="italic">ready</hi> to say, He will not come, and <hi type="italic">unready</hi> to meet him. (4.) His coming will indeed be <hi type="italic">coming suddenly;</hi> it will be a great <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> and <hi type="italic">terror</hi> to those that are careless, and asleep, it will come upon them as a thief in the night. (5.) It is therefore the indispensable duty of all Christ's disciples, to <hi type="italic">watch,</hi> to be awake, and keep awake; "<hi type="italic">What I say unto you</hi> four (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">v. 37</reference>), I <hi type="italic">say unto all</hi> the twelve, or rather to <hi type="italic">you</hi> twelve, I say unto all my disciples and followers; what I say to you of this generation, I say to all that shall believe in men, through your word, in every age, <hi type="italic">Watch, watch,</hi> expect my second coming, prepare for it, that you may be found in peace, without spot, and blameless."  <chapter eID="Mark.13"/> <div eID="gen24909" type="x-p"/>

entries.37d01303c1383bf71e1ab4c15eba308919b8e0a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14124"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.13.1-Mark.13.37">Mr 13:1-37</reference>. Christ's Prophecy of the Destruction of Jerusalem, and Warnings Suggested by It to Prepare for His Second Coming. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.24.1-Matt.24.51">Mt 24:1-51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.5-Luke.21.36">Lu 21:5-36</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus had uttered all His mind against the Jewish ecclesiastics, exposing their character with withering plainness, and denouncing, in language of awful severity, the judgments of God against them for that unfaithfulness to their trust which was bringing ruin upon the nation. He had closed this His last public discourse (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39">Mt 23:1-39</reference>) by a passionate lamentation over Jerusalem, and a solemn farewell to the temple. "And," says Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.1">Mt 24:1</reference>), "Jesus went out and departed from the temple"--</hi>never more to re-enter its precincts, or open His mouth in public teaching. With this act ended His public ministry. As He withdrew, says Olshausen, the gracious presence of God left the sanctuary; and the temple, with all its service, and the whole theocratic constitution, was given over to destruction. What immediately followed is, as usual, most minutely and graphically described by our Evangelist.<div eID="gen27290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14124"/><hi type="bold">1. And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him--</hi>The other Evangelists are less definite. "As some spake," says Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.5">Lu 21:5</reference>); "His disciples came to Him," says Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.2">Mt 24:2</reference>). Doubtless it was the speech of one, the mouthpiece, likely, of others.<div eID="gen27291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Master--</hi>Teacher.<div eID="gen27292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">see what manner of stones and what buildings are here--</hi>wondering probably, how so massive a pile could be overthrown, as seemed implied in our Lord's last words regarding it. Josephus, who gives a minute account of the wonderful structure, speaks of stones forty cubits long [Wars of the Jews, 5.5.1.] and says the pillars supporting the porches were twenty-five cubits high, all of one stone, and that of the whitest marble [Wars of the Jews, 5.5.2]. Six days' battering at the walls, during the siege, made no impression upon them [Wars of the Jews, 6.4.1]. Some of the under-building, yet remaining, and other works, are probably as old as the first temple. <div eID="gen27293" type="x-p"/>
entries.eaa972bbec54b10020868894ef4946d9a092cdac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14125"/><div sID="gen27294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14125"/><hi type="bold">2. And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings?--</hi>"Ye call My attention to these things? I have seen them. Ye point to their massive and durable appearance: now listen to their fate."<div eID="gen27294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall not be left--</hi>"left here" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.2">Mt 24:2</reference>).<div eID="gen27295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down--</hi>Titus ordered the whole city and temple to be demolished [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 7.1.1]; Eleazar wished they had all died before seeing that holy city destroyed by enemies' hands, and before the temple was so profanely dug up [Wars of the Jews, 7.8.7]. <div eID="gen27296" type="x-p"/>
entries.c70129b7378cb14a3361209b3b96c8a8db090af9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14126"/><div sID="gen27297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14126"/><hi type="bold">3. And as he sat upon the Mount of Olives, over against the temple--</hi>On their way from Jerusalem to Bethany they would cross Mount Olivet; on its summit He seats Himself, over against the temple, having the city all spread out under His eye. How graphically is this set before us by our Evangelist!<div eID="gen27297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately--</hi>The other Evangelists tell us merely that "the disciples" did so. entries.0f19f1b4bd4f4a7323ed230e36183c2cc61935af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14127"/><div sID="gen27299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14127"/><hi type="bold">4. Tell us, when shall these things be? and what shall be the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled?--</hi>"and what shall be the sign of Thy coming, and of the end of the world?" Our Lord takes His own way of meeting their questions.<div eID="gen27299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27300" type="x-p"/> Prophecies of the Destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.5-Mark.13.31">Mr 13:5-31</reference>). <div eID="gen27300" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa6618483929aea34c46964ebef9a519be450a33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14128"/><div sID="gen27301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14128"/>5. entries.4a82b1ab5db1c86d4d5a6c30ded47670f1f3e59c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14129"/><div sID="gen27302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14129"/><hi type="bold">6. For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Mt 24:5</reference>)--"and the time draweth nigh" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.8">Lu 21:8</reference>); that is, the time of the kingdom in its full splendor.<div eID="gen27302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and shall deceive many--</hi>"Go ye not therefore after them" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.8">Lu 21:8</reference>). The reference here seems not to be to pretended Messiahs, deceiving those who rejected the claims of Jesus, of whom indeed there were plenty--for our Lord is addressing His own genuine disciples--but to persons pretending to be Jesus Himself, returned in glory to take possession of His kingdom. This gives peculiar force to the words, "Go ye not therefore after them." <div eID="gen27303" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7a5ef3f18f3960fe97f2abc991ecd34835948eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14130"/><div sID="gen27304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14130"/><hi type="bold">7. entries.3ac997ea70ecd3551ea6d428ce70db3f61ce0dbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14131"/><div sID="gen27306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14131"/><hi type="bold">8. The annals of Tacitus tell us how the Roman world was convulsed, before the destruction of Jerusalem, by rival claimants of the imperial purple. <div eID="gen27306" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fa4cede6cdf586e650b11e8b4cbf0102966249c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14132"/><div sID="gen27307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14132"/><hi type="bold">9. But take heed to yourselves: for--</hi>"before all these things" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.12">Lu 21:12</reference>); that is, before these public calamities come.<div eID="gen27307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten--</hi>These refer to ecclesiastical proceedings against them.<div eID="gen27308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings--</hi>before civil tribunals next.<div eID="gen27309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for my sake, for a testimony against them--</hi>rather "unto them"--to give you an opportunity of bearing testimony to Me before them. In the Acts of the Apostles we have the best commentary on this announcement. (Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.10.17">Mt 10:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen27310" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f78fded42ce24df5daea490e6f7e5f828ac45d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14133"/><div sID="gen27311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14133"/><hi type="bold">10. And the gospel must first be published among all nations--</hi>"for a witness, and then shall the end come" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Mt 24:14</reference>). God never sends judgment without previous warning; and there can be no doubt that the Jews, already dispersed over most known countries, had nearly all heard the Gospel "as a witness," before the end of the Jewish state. The same principle was repeated and will repeat itself to "the end." <div eID="gen27311" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1ca106a4e3972d74c5a0dfcc1322f8dfcb197ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14134"/><div sID="gen27312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14134"/><hi type="bold">11. But when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand--</hi>"Be not anxious beforehand."<div eID="gen27312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate--</hi>"Be not filled with apprehension, in the prospect of such public appearances for Me, lest ye should bring discredit upon My name, nor think it necessary to prepare beforehand what ye are to say."<div eID="gen27313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Mt 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">20</reference>.) <div eID="gen27314" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0d1cad5e7f78bd17f1e907e079397258b0200d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14135"/><div sID="gen27315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14135"/><hi type="bold">13. And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.12">Mt 24:12</reference>) adds this important intimation: "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many"--"of the many," or "of the most," that is, of the generality of professed disciples--"shall wax cold." Sad illustrations of the effect of abounding iniquity in cooling the love even of faithful disciples we have in the Epistle of James, written about the period here referred to, and too frequently ever since.<div eID="gen27315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.21">Mt 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">22</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">39</reference>, which is a manifest allusion to these words of Christ; also <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">Lu 21:18</reference>) adds these reassuring words: "But there shall not an hair of your heads perish." Our Lord had just said (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.16">Lu 21:16</reference>) that they should be put to death; showing that this precious promise is far above immunity from mere bodily harm, and furnishing a key to the right interpretation of Psa 91:1-18 and such like. <div eID="gen27316" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a2e421006bd2622c75e1f5330550af4d46babb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14136"/><div sID="gen27317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14136"/><hi type="bold">14. But when ye shall see--</hi>"Jerusalem compassed by armies"--by encamped armies; in other words, when ye shall see it besieged, and<div eID="gen27317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not--</hi>that is, as explained in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Mt 24:15</reference>), "standing in the holy place."<div eID="gen27318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">(let him that readeth understand)--</hi>readeth that prophecy. That "the abomination of desolation" here alluded to was intended to point to the Roman ensigns, as the symbols of an idolatrous, and so unclean pagan power, may be gathered by comparing what Luke says in the corresponding verse (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.20">Lu 21:20</reference>); and commentators are agreed on it. It is worthy of notice, as confirming this interpretation, that in 1 Maccabees 1:54--which, though aprocryphal Scripture, is authentic history--the expression of Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">Da 11:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.11">12:11</reference>) is applied to the idolatrous profanation of the Jewish altar by Antiochus Epiphanes.<div eID="gen27319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then let them that be in Judea flee to the mountains--</hi>The ecclesiastical historian, Eusebius, early in the fourth century, tells us that the Christians fled to Pella, at the northern extremity of Perea, being "prophetically directed"--perhaps by some prophetic intimation more explicit than this, which would be their chart--and that thus they escaped the predicted calamities by which the nation was overwhelmed. <div eID="gen27320" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ed4d2c2d75240ab7fc3737acb56d139bcb31c07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14137"/><div sID="gen27321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14137"/><hi type="bold">15. entries.e1e92c35f3783c0100035f3462e744b2d5f1853c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14141"/><div sID="gen27326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14141"/><hi type="bold">19. For in those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created unto this time, neither shall be--</hi>Such language is not unusual in the Old Testament with reference to tremendous calamities. But it is matter of literal fact that there was crowded into the period of the Jewish war an amount and complication of suffering perhaps unparalleled; as the narrative of Josephus, examined closely and arranged under different heads, would show. <div eID="gen27326" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dc7a3b3ee5bf01ec1b9690f16d692c55db5911f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14142"/><div sID="gen27327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14142"/><hi type="bold">20. And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh--</hi>that is, no human life.<div eID="gen27327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">should be saved: but for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days--</hi>But for this merciful "shortening," brought about by a remarkable concurrence of causes, the whole nation would have perished, in which there yet remained a remnant to be afterwards gathered out. This portion of the prophecy closes, in Luke, with the following vivid and important glance at the subsequent fortunes of the chosen people: "And they shall fall by the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations: and Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.24">Lu 21:24</reference>). The language as well as the idea of this remarkable statement is taken from <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Da 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">13</reference>. What, then, is its import here? It implies, first, that a time is coming when Jerusalem shall cease to be "trodden down of the Gentiles"; which it was then by pagan, and since and till now is by Mohammedan unbelievers: and next, it implies that the period when this treading down of Jerusalem by the Gentiles is to cease will be when "the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" or "completed." But what does this mean? We may gather the meaning of it from <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1-Rom.11.36">Ro 11:1-36</reference> in which the divine purposes and procedure towards the chosen people from first to last are treated in detail. In <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference> these words of our Lord are thus reproduced: "For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in." See the exposition of that verse, from which it will appear that "till the fulness of the Gentiles be come in"--or, in our Lord's phraseology, "till the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled"--does not mean "till the general conversion of the world to Christ," but "till the Gentiles have had their full time of that place in the Church which the Jews had before them." After that period of Gentilism, as before of Judaism, "Jerusalem" and Israel, no longer "trodden down by the Gentiles," but "grafted into their own olive tree," shall constitute, with the believing Gentiles, one Church of God, and fill the whole earth. What a bright vista does this open up! <div eID="gen27328" type="x-p"/>

entries.f6b1a833e55a4c49b2533672ad7a2186ca6e62ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14144"/><div sID="gen27330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14144"/>22. For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall show signs and wonders. No one can read Josephus' account of what took place before the destruction of Jerusalem without seeing how strikingly this was fulfilled.<div eID="gen27330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to seduce, if it were possible, even the elect--</hi>implying that this, though all but done, will prove impossible. What a precious assurance! (Compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:9-12</reference>). <div eID="gen27331" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf6cc7a7a23530f767e4fb73db4494ae0793eb43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14145"/><div sID="gen27332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14145"/><hi type="bold">23. But take ye heed; behold, I have foretold you all things--</hi>He had just told them that the seduction of the elect would prove impossible; but since this would be all but accomplished, He bids them be on their guard, as the proper means of averting that catastrophe. In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.26-Matt.24.28">Mt 24:26-28</reference>) we have some additional particulars: "Wherefore, if they shall say unto you, Behold, He is in the desert; go not forth: behold, He is in the secret chambers; believe it not. For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be." See on <reference osisRef="Luke.17.23">Lu 17:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.24">24</reference>. "For wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together." See on <reference osisRef="Luke.17.37">Lu 17:37</reference>. <div eID="gen27332" type="x-p"/>
